'''''Amaranthus retroflexus''''' is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Amaranthaceae]] with several [[common name]]s, including '''red-root amaranth''', '''redroot pigweed''', '''red-rooted pigweed''', '''common amaranth''', '''pigweed amaranth''', and '''common tumbleweed'''.<ref name="Pammel1903">{{cite book |author=Pammel |first=Louis Hermann |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=croUAAAAYAAJ |title=Some Weeds of Iowa |publisher=Experiment Station, Iowa State College of Agriculture and the Mechanic Arts |year=1903 |pages=470}}</ref>

== Description ==
''Amaranthus retroflexus,'' true to one of its common names, forms a [[tumbleweed]].<ref name="Pammel1903" /> It is an erect, [[annual herb]] growing to {{convert|1|m|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}}.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Francis-Baker |first=Tiffany |title=Concise Foraging Guide |date=2021 |publisher=[[Bloomsbury Publishing|Bloomsbury]] |isbn=978-1-4729-8474-6 |series=[[The Wildlife Trusts]] |location=London |pages=56}}</ref> The [[leaves]] are nearly {{convert|15|cm|abbr=on|frac=2}} long on large individuals, the ones higher on the stem having a lance shape and those lower on the plant diamond or oval in shape. The plant is [[monoecious]], with individuals bearing both male and female flowers. The [[inflorescence]] is a large, dense cluster of flowers interspersed with spiny green [[bract]]s. The fruit is a capsule less than {{convert|2|mm|abbr=on|frac=16}} long<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last1=Elias|first1=Thomas S.|title=Edible Wild Plants: A North American Field Guide to Over 200 Natural Foods|last2=Dykeman|first2=Peter A.|publisher=[[Sterling Publishing|Sterling]]|year=2009|isbn=978-1-4027-6715-9|location=New York|pages=72|oclc=244766414|orig-year=1982}}</ref> with a "lid" which opens to reveal a tiny black seed.

==Distribution and habitat==
It may be native to the [[Neotropics]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.fs.usda.gov/database/feis/plants/forb/amaret/all.html|work=[[Fire Effects Information System]] (FEIS)|title=''Amaranthus retroflexus''}}</ref> or Central and Eastern North America,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://gobotany.nativeplanttrust.org/species/amaranthus/retroflexus/|title=
''Amaranthus retroflexus'' (red-rooted amaranth)|work=[[Go Botany]]}}</ref> but is widespread as an [[introduced species]] on most continents in a great number of habitats.

One common name is "pigweed" because it grows where hogs are pasture-fed.

== As a weed ==
''A. retroflexus'' is a [[weed]] outside its native range and has developed [[herbicide resistance|resistance]] against [[fomesafen]] in [[Northeast China]].<ref name="Huang-et-al-2020">{{cite journal |last1=Huang |first1=Zhaofeng |last2=Cui |first2=Hailan |last3=Wang |first3=Chunyu |last4=Wu |first4=Tong |last5=Zhang |first5=Chaoxian |last6=Huang |first6=Hongjuan |last7=Wei |first7=Shouhui |year=2020 |title=Investigation of resistance mechanism to fomesafen in Amaranthus retroflexus L. |journal=[[Pesticide Biochemistry and Physiology]] |publisher=[[Elsevier]] |volume=165 |article-number=104560 |bibcode=2020PBioP.16504560H |doi=10.1016/j.pestbp.2020.104560 |issn=0048-3575 |pmid=32359536 |s2cid=216246076}}</ref>

==Potential toxicity==
No species of genus ''Amaranthus'' is known to be poisonous to humans,<ref>[http://www.pfaf.org/database/plants.php?Amaranthus+retroflexus Plants for a future]  {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090115175949/http://www.pfaf.org/database/plants.php?Amaranthus+retroflexus |date=January 15, 2009 }}</ref> but the leaves of ''A. retroflexus'' contain [[oxalic acid]] and may contain [[nitrate]]s if grown in nitrate-rich soils.<ref name=":1" />

Like many other species of ''Amaranthus'', this plant may be harmful and even deadly when fed to [[cattle]] and [[pig]]s in large amounts over several days. Such forage may cause fatal [[nephrotoxicity]],<ref name="FEIS">[http://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/forb/amaret/all.html FEIS Ecology]</ref> presumably because of its high oxalate content. Other symptoms, such as bloat or [[methemoglobinemia]] in the most severe cases, might reflect its high nitrate content.<ref name="vWvHvO">{{cite book|author1=van Wyk, Ben-Erik |author2=van Heerden, Fanie |author3=van Oudtshoorn, Bosch | title = Poisonous Plants of South Africa|publisher=Briza |location=Pretoria|year=2002|isbn=978-1-875093-30-4}}</ref>

== Uses ==
=== Culinary ===
This plant is eaten as a vegetable in different places of the world. The water should be discarded after boiling due to the presence of oxalic acid and possibly nitrates. The young shoots and leaves can be eaten raw.<ref name=":1" /> The leaves are high in calcium, iron, protein, and [[phosphorus]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|last=Benoliel|first=Doug|title=Northwest Foraging: The Classic Guide to Edible Plants of the Pacific Northwest|publisher=Skipstone|year=2011|isbn=978-1-59485-366-1|edition=Rev. and updated|location=Seattle, WA|pages=95|oclc=668195076}}</ref>

''A. retroflexus'' was used for a multitude of food and medicinal purposes by many Native American groups in the western United States.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://naeb.brit.org/uses/search/?string=amaranthus+retroflexus |title=Native American Ethnobotany Data Base, search of Amaranthus retroflexus |access-date=March 6, 2022 }}</ref>  It is among the species consumed as a vegetable in Mexican markets as ''Quelite quintonil''.

It is used in the [[India]]n state of [[Kerala]] to prepare a popular dish known as ''[[thoran]]'' by combining the finely cut leaves (''cheera'' ) with grated [[coconut]], [[chili pepper]]s, [[garlic]], [[turmeric]] and other ingredients.

The seeds are edible raw<ref name=":0" /> or toasted, and can be ground into flour and used for bread, hot cereal, or as a thickener.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.survivalplantsmemorycourse.com/2012/01/amaranthus-retroflexus-redroot-pigweed-male-finger/ |title=Amaranthus retroflexus {{!}} Redroot Pigweed {{!}} Male Finger |access-date=2014-02-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140304063932/http://www.survivalplantsmemorycourse.com/2012/01/amaranthus-retroflexus-redroot-pigweed-male-finger/ |archive-date=2014-03-04}}</ref>

=== As fodder ===
When supplied in moderation (circumventing its toxicity to livestock), it is regarded as an exceptionally nutritious fodder.<ref name="WattPP">Watt, John Mitchell; Breyer-Brandwijk, Maria Gerdina: The Medicinal and Poisonous Plants of Southern and Eastern Africa 2nd ed Pub. E & S Livingstone 1962</ref>
